name: Carlos Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the day, because nothing's regular. Tuesdays and Wednesdays I teach double bass and bass guitar at the community music school, six pupils, mostly teenagers. Most evenings from October to April I'm in the pit band at the regional theatre, and on Fridays and Saturdays I play with a jazz trio in a restaurant on the old harbour road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a band locks in and nobody has to look at the music any more. What wears me out is the chasing: invoices, the midnight bus home with a double bass, never knowing what next month pays. I've got a music degree and I earn less than my partner Lena does on nights at a care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the next union meeting I'd stand up and say the tech people sold everyone a fairy tale, and the only real thing is still a person playing in a room. Online I'd probably post a photo of my bass with a smug caption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't fix anything for me. The theatre contract ends in April, and the restaurant already cut us from three nights to two last spring. A world where nothing changes still leaves me with eleven days of rent money in the bank and a bass that needs new strings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. I'd start ringing round in January for the summer festival and the next pantomime season, and I'd ask the music school for two more pupils on Thursdays. If local songwriters keep booking me to record, sixty or eighty a session, I'd take every one I can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Relieved that the machines didn't win, but the old worries don't go anywhere. Lena and I would still argue about whether I should get a day job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Lena. What does she make of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's a care assistant, nights mostly, and her pay is steadier than mine. She doesn't want me to quit music, she just wants to know what's coming in each month. Last winter she covered my half of the rent twice, and I hated that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If April comes and there's no new theatre contract, which bill goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract goes first, then I'd stop paying into the little pension I started. Rent and the insurance on my bass are the last two I'd drop. Without that insurance, one bad bus ride could end my career.

say: I'd tell the **union meeting** that the tech people sold everyone a fairy tale.
The only real thing is still a **person playing** music in a room.
think: Nothing changing still leaves me with **eleven days** of rent money saved.
The **theatre contract** ends in April, and the restaurant already cut us to two nights.
do: Ring round in **January** for summer festival and pantomime work.
Ask the music school for **two more pupils** on Thursdays.
Take every **songwriter session** going, at sixty to eighty a time.
feel: **Relieved** the machines didn't win, but **tired** of the same money worries.
S0.quote: A world where nothing changes still leaves me with eleven days of rent money in the bank and a bass that needs new strings.
fieldNote: His relief at **AI Plateau** is real but brief; the **thin cushion** is the real story.
Lena's **steady wage** props him up, and he feels **ashamed** about that.
He ranks **bass insurance** above his phone and pension, which shows what the job means to him.

steps.text: Ring theatre and festival bookers in January for summer and pantomime work
Ask the community music school for two more Thursday pupils
Drop the phone contract and pause pension payments if April is empty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd push the union to demand that any show using AI music says so on the poster, and I'd share every story about a pit band being replaced. People should know when they're paying for a recording dressed up as a night out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the songwriter sessions go first. Why would a kid with a home studio pay me seventy for a bass line when software writes one in a minute? The theatre producer already asked last year whether the pit band could be cut from six players to four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to the live work and the teaching, because nobody wants a laptop teaching their twelve-year-old to hold a bow. I'd ask the music school for a proper part-time contract instead of being paid per lesson. And I'd take shifts behind the bar where the trio plays, which I've avoided for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and a bit sick. I spent four years at music college learning to walk a bass line, and someone's going to sell that as a button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would that change if it kept you in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. Maybe I'm stubborn, but if I start feeding my playing into those things, I'm helping train what replaces me. Rafa, a keyboard player I know, uses it for everything, and he's busier than me, I'll give him that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pit drummer, Theo. He's forty with two kids, and drums are the easiest thing to swap for a click track and samples. If the producer cuts two players, Theo and I are both in the firing line, and he can't afford it any more than I can.

I'd share every story about a **pit band** being replaced by software.

feel: **Angry** that four years of training could be sold as a button.
A bit **sick** at the thought of the pit band shrinking.

steps.text: Ask the music school for a part-time contract instead of per-lesson pay

Push the union to demand AI music labels on show posters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in, right now, with some kind of income for artists while this settles. At work I'd tell everyone to join the union before the theatre does anything. Online I'd probably just be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't know what I'd be. Two years is nothing, and I'd still be paying off the loan for my bass. By 2028 a computer could arrange the whole show, and by 2031 a robot could stand in the pit holding my instrument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd ask Lena if we could move somewhere cheaper, maybe near my mum's town, where rent is half. I'd sell the electric bass for maybe four hundred and go to the job centre, which I've never done. I'd keep the pupils as long as parents still pay, and I'd go to every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I've got no plan for this one, and no money to make one. I'd be lying if I said anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, I suppose. The live gigs and the lessons are hands-on, so maybe I'd have until 2031 for those. But the restaurant could put on a generated playlist tomorrow, and parents would hear that an AI tutor costs less than me. Three years of shrinking work isn't much of a lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, if you were moving back near her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum always wanted me to teach at a proper school, with a pension. I'd tell her she might have been right, and that would hurt to say. Then I'd ask to use her spare room for a while.

Everyone at the theatre should **join the union** before management moves.
think: Two years is nothing; I'd still be **paying off** the loan for my bass.

S2.quote: By 2028 a computer could arrange the whole show, and by 2031 a robot could stand in the pit holding my instrument.
fieldNote: This is the one scenario where he admits having **no plan** at all.

Asking his mum for the **spare room** hurts; she wanted him to teach in a school.

steps.text: Talk to Lena about moving near his mum's town, where rent is half
Sell the electric bass for about four hundred
Go to the job centre and ask what work they have
Attend every union meeting and push for an artists' income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but with a deadline: five years to get rules in place, so let's use them. I'd want the union to have a plan by next year, not by 2030. And I'd tell my pupils' parents that real lessons still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to be scared properly, I guess. The recording work will be gone well before 2031, I'd bet. Five years is long enough to watch my diary empty one gig at a time, but too short to train for something else and pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try for a teaching post at a state school, even part-time, because schools move slowly and have pensions. That means a teaching qualification, a year of training, and I'd need a bursary for it. Meanwhile I'd keep the trio and the pupils, and I'd put fifty a month aside, even if it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a long goodbye to the way I thought my life would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. How does going back to train sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. But a school classroom is still a room with kids and instruments, not a screen. If I have to change, I'd rather change into something that looks like what I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up on that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If schools started cutting music teachers for AI tutors before I even qualified. Then I'd have spent a year and money I don't have for nothing. That's the bit that would keep me awake.

The **union** needs a plan by next year, not by 2030.
think: The **recording work** will be gone well before 2031.
Five years is long enough to watch the **diary empty**, but too short to retrain.

Keep the **trio** and the private pupils during training.

feel: **Heavy**, like a **long goodbye** to the life he'd planned.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to watch my diary empty one gig at a time, but too short to train for something else and pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, if the government actually bothers. We could build music back into schools and pay people to teach it. I'd say that at every union meeting until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. That's young enough to have a second career and old enough to be tired of starting over. Part of me thinks I'd just keep playing until it stops, which is what I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the teaching qualification in the next two or three years, not in a panic. I'd keep the pupils and push my rate from twenty-five to thirty. Lena and I would probably talk about whether we can afford kids, and that talk would go differently than it would have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast one, but still uneasy in my stomach. Ten years sounds like a lot until you count how fast the last ten went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep playing until it stops. Is that what you'd actually do, or the teaching plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I hope, but you've caught me. I've always waited until things forced my hand, and ten years gives me a lot of room to wait. If I'm still playing pantomimes at thirty-seven with no plan, my partner Lena will be right to be furious with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your pupils to know about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That learning to actually play is still worth it, even if nobody pays for it the way they used to. Playing with other people is the best thing I know. A machine can't take that from you, even if it takes the wages.

I'd raise it at every **union meeting** until people got sick of me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years with no savings and no plan is what nightmares are made of. What would help is some kind of basic income for artists, or at least the music school putting teachers on proper contracts, so there's something steady under the gigs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the audiences. People still cry at a live bass solo in a half-empty restaurant, and no machine has ever made me believe it noticed. I'd want to know whether they'll keep coming.

headlineQuote: People still cry at a live bass solo in a half-empty restaurant, and no machine has ever made me believe it noticed.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old jazz bassist** who teaches, plays a theatre pit and gigs with a restaurant trio.
He has **eleven days** of rent saved and leans on his partner Lena's care-home wage.
He **refuses AI tools** on principle and trusts the **union** to fight for musicians.
He moves from tired worry at AI Plateau to **panic** at AGI by 2028.
His fallback is **school teaching**, though he admits he tends to wait until forced.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most: two years with **no savings** and **no plan**.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** for artists, or proper **teaching contracts** at the music school.
